abstract: |
  The murderer at the door is Benjamin Constant's example, introduced in 1797 to illustrate a theory of principles on which a principle's essence is not generality but fixity: a principle yields the same result whenever the same combination recurs, and so is a rule people can count on, as against the arbitrary. Read inside that theory, Constant's own resolution of the case, that no one has a right to a truth that harms others, is a specification rather than an exception, but it is keyed to harm, and so fails his own test: it makes each speaker judge of circumstances, and it releases the witness whose testimony convicts the guilty. Kant's reply, that an exception makes the law "wavering and useless" and that Constant confused harming with wronging, is in this respect an internal critique. The pamphlet shows the case Constant had in mind, the proscribed man seeking asylum, and an 1815 note on Rousseau states the principle that case needed: "when pretended laws demand the truth of us only to proscribe us, we do not owe them the truth." # Constant's example {#sec-intro}

The example now called "the murderer at the door" is not Kant's. In the eighth chapter of *Des réactions politiques*, a pamphlet signed at Hérivaux on 10 germinal year V (30 March 1797), Benjamin Constant wrote that "a German philosopher" goes so far as to claim "that towards assassins who asked you whether your friend, whom they are pursuing, has not taken refuge in your house, a lie would be a crime" [@Constant1797, 74].^[Translations from Constant and Kant are mine. References to @Constant1797 are by page alone after this note; Kant is cited by volume and page of the Akademie edition [@KantAA], the *Critique of Pure Reason* by B-pagination.] Kant read the passage in Carl Friedrich Cramer's German translation, admitted in a note that he had said something of the kind (8:425), and replied that autumn in "On a Supposed Right to Lie from Love of Humanity". The reply became one of the most discussed short texts in moral philosophy, and Constant became its foil.

He has played two parts. In one he is the voice of expediency, for whom a principle yields when following it is dangerous; the title of @Benton1982, "Political Expediency and Lying", names the part. In the other, familiar to readers who meet the case through Kant's restatement, he holds that the murderer has forfeited his right to the truth. Neither part fits the chapter. Constant introduces the example to illustrate a theory of what principles are and how they apply, and the theory is as hostile to expediency as Kant's: "a principle recognized as true must therefore never be abandoned, whatever its apparent dangers" (77), a sentence Kant quotes with approval (8:428). And the principle Constant draws from the case says nothing about forfeiture. It says that "no man has a right to a truth that harms others" (76).

This paper reads the exchange with Constant at its centre, and argues for four claims. First, Constant's theory makes the essence of a principle its *fixity*, not its generality: a principle yields the same result whenever the same combination of facts recurs, and is therefore a rule people can count on, as against the arbitrary (@sec-principles). Second, Constant's resolution of his example is, by that theory, a specification rather than an exception, but it is keyed to harm, and a rule so keyed is not fixed by his own standard (@sec-example). Kant's charges that an exception makes the law "wavering and useless" (8:427) and that Constant confused harming with wronging (8:428) are, in this respect, an internal critique (@sec-kant). Third, the pamphlet shows what case Constant had in mind, the proscribed man seeking asylum, and a note of 1815 states the principle that case needed, keyed not to harm but to the title of whoever demands the truth: "when pretended laws demand the truth of us only to proscribe us, we do not owe them the truth" (@sec-needed). That principle passes both Constant's test and Kant's distinction, and it meets Kant on the ground he chose, the declaration made under compulsion. Fourth, what then remains between the two men is a disagreement about authority, not about principles (@sec-remains).

Parts of this have precedents. @Zupancic1993 [179] noted that Constant "nowhere uses the word exception"; @Loparic2006 [63–65] quoted the definition of a principle as fixed and set it against Kant's a priori principles, though he still read Constant's restriction as an exception. Several readers place the example in the Revolution, where, in Wood's summary of @Holmes1984, "the line separating police officials from murderers was not necessarily well-defined" [@Wood2011], and @Troitsky2016 connects Kant's verdict to his denial of a right of resistance. What I add is the use of Constant's own theory to assess his resolution, the 1815 note, and a reading of the "right to the truth" as a matter of jurisdiction.

# What a principle is {#sec-principles}

*Des réactions politiques* defends the republican constitution of year III against the reactions that followed the Terror, both the reaction against the Terror's crimes and the reaction against the ideas in whose name they were committed. Its seventh to ninth chapters defend principles against two opponents: those who exaggerate principles until they become inapplicable, and those who conclude from the excesses that principles are useless. The second group is led by Burke, named in chapter IX for holding that axioms "metaphysically true" can be "politically false" (81).

Chapter VIII, "Des principes", begins with a definition:

> A principle is the general result of a certain number of particular facts. Whenever the set of these facts undergoes some change, the principle that resulted from it is modified; but then this modification itself becomes a principle. (66)

Everything in the universe has its principles, because every combination of existences or events leads to a result, "and this result is always the same, whenever the combinations are the same" (66). Such a result "is general only in relation to the combinations from which it results. It is therefore general only in a relative and not an absolute way. This distinction is of great importance" (66). There are universal principles, because some data are present in all combinations, but to them must be added principles "resulting from each particular combination" (67). Those who call general principles inapplicable mean only that the intermediate principle the combination requires has not been found: "one of the links of the chain" is lost, but the chain exists (67). Then comes the central claim:

> Secondary principles are just as immutable as first principles. Each interruption of the great chain has only one link to fill it. … Each circumstance calls only for the principle proper to it, for the essence of a principle is not to be general, nor applicable to many cases, but to be fixed; and this quality so far makes up its essence that all its utility resides in it. (67–68)

Two properties are distinguished here. A principle's *generality* is its breadth, the range of cases it covers. Its *fixity* has two aspects in the chapter. One is formal: like combinations, like results. The other is practical: a fixed principle can be relied on, which is why "all its utility" lies in fixity. Chapter IX, "De l'arbitraire", makes the practical aspect explicit. The arbitrary is "the absence of rules, of limits, of definitions, in a word the absence of all that is precise" (80), and morality is "an assemblage of rules on which individuals must be able to count mutually in their social relations" (82). Without principles, "there is nothing fixed: only circumstances remain, and each person is judge of the circumstances"; where "everything is wavering, no fulcrum is possible" (78).

Kant had his own terms for the first contrast. Experience gives its judgements "only assumed and comparative universality (through induction)", while strict universality, which "allows no exception as possible", marks the a priori (B3–4). Constant's principles, "general results" of facts, are comparatively universal in exactly this sense, and he says so. What he denies is that it matters. A principle's authority comes neither from its breadth nor from its source but from the fixed connection between a type of combination and a result. In later terms he separates universality from generality, as Hare did when he wrote that "generality is the opposite of specificity, whereas universalizability is compatible with specificity" [@Hare1981, 41]. But the period's own contrast is the better guide, and Kant uses it at the decisive point: intermediate principles may contain "the closer determination [*nähere Bestimmung*] of their application to cases", but "never exceptions" (8:430).

The chapter's model is political. That "no man can be bound except by laws to whose formation he has contributed" is a universal principle; in a large society it is applied through an intermediate principle, that individuals may contribute "either in person or through their representatives" (72). Someone who applied the first principle to a large society without the second would overthrow it, but that would prove "nothing against the principle" (72). Kant calls this remark "well thought and at the same time correct" (8:427), and restates the example as an axiom, a postulate and a problem whose solution is the representative system (8:429). He had made the general point himself four years earlier: when theory is of little use in practice, "it was not the fault of the theory, but that there was not enough theory" (8:275).

What Constant took to be new was a method. An intermediate principle is found by *defining* the principle that seems inapplicable, "surveying its whole circumference", until we find "the link that unites it to another principle" (74–75). "It is an idea perhaps new, but which seems to me infinitely important, that every principle contains, either in itself or in its relation to another principle, its means of application" (77). Here Kant and Constant part, though Kant never says so. In the same passage of 1793 Kant insists that between a rule and its application there must be an act of judgement, for which rules cannot always be given, "because that would go on to infinity" (8:275). Constant's method is an attempt to do without that act: the chain of principles, completed by definition, would leave nothing to judgement. I return to this in @sec-remains.

# The example inside the theory {#sec-example}

Constant turns to morality as the better case. Morality is "a science much more advanced than politics", because the need for it is daily and its intermediate principles are better known (73). Yet its abstract principles, separated from their intermediate principles, would cause as much disorder in social relations as the abstract principles of politics cause in civil ones. Then the example:

> The moral principle, for example, that telling the truth is a duty, if it were taken in an absolute and isolated way, would make all society impossible. We have the proof of this in the very direct consequences that a German philosopher has drawn from this principle, who goes so far as to claim that towards assassins who asked you whether your friend, whom they are pursuing, has not taken refuge in your house, a lie would be a crime. (74)

The details matter. The questioners are plural assassins; the person sought is "your friend", who has "taken refuge" in your house. There is no stipulation that you must answer yes or no, or that a lie may misfire. Those are Kant's additions (8:426–427), made to a translation in which Constant's assassins had become "a murderer" (8:425).

The case is set up as a dilemma. The principle in isolation "is inapplicable. It would destroy society. But if you reject it, society will be no less destroyed, for all the foundations of morality will be overturned" (75). Constant thus shares Kant's premise that truthfulness is a foundation of social life. The way out is definition:

> Telling the truth is a duty. What is a duty? The idea of duty is inseparable from that of rights: a duty is what, in one being, corresponds to the rights of another. Where there are no rights, there are no duties. Telling the truth is therefore a duty only towards those who have a right to the truth. But no man has a right to a truth that harms others. (75–76)

"There, it seems to me, is the principle become applicable" (76). This is offered as no concession to circumstance. The man who, "struck by the inconveniences of the principle", declaimed against abstractions instead of defining it "would have thrown everything into the arbitrary". By defining it "we have found the precise modification of the principle of truth, which excludes all arbitrariness and all uncertainty" (76–77).

By Constant's lights this is not an exception. On the definition of p. 66, when the facts change "this modification itself becomes a principle", and the restricted duty is such a modification, "just as immutable" as the duty it restricts. Zupančič is right that the word "exception" does not appear. The question Constant's theory makes pressing is a different one: whether the modification is fixed. That depends on what it is keyed to.

It is keyed to harm. The clause does not say that those who would use the truth for a crime lose their right to it, or that assassins are owed nothing. It says that no one has a right to a truth "qui nuit à autrui", a truth that harms someone other than the questioner. The assassins drop out of the statement of the principle; what decides is the truth's effect on the friend. Readers who come to the case through Kant's restatement often credit Constant with a principle of forfeiture, on which the would-be murderer has lost his claim by his intent. Such a principle would make the case turn on the questioner. Constant's 1797 principle makes it turn on consequences.

# Kant's reply, read from Constant's side {#sec-kant}

Kant's reply is usually read as a defence of an exceptionless duty against a consequentialist. Read with chapter VIII in view, it is closer to an argument on shared ground.

The common ground is larger than it looks. Kant accepts Constant's methodological remark and his political example (8:427–429). His last sentence states a criterion Constant accepts: intermediate principles "can contain only the closer determination of their application to cases that arise … but never exceptions from them, because these destroy the universality on account of which alone they bear the name of principles" (8:430). And Kant concedes the point about the questioner. "Although I do no wrong to him who unjustly compels me to a statement if I falsify it", I do wrong "in the most essential part of duty in general", by bringing it about, so far as I can, that statements in general find no belief and that rights founded on contracts lose their force: "a wrong done to humanity in general" (8:426). Kant agrees that the questioner is not wronged. His objection is that someone else is.

Where they part, Kant says that Constant "had himself abandoned" the unconditional principle of truthfulness "because of the danger it brings to society: because he could not discover an intermediate principle that would serve to prevent this danger, and here none can really be inserted" (8:428). As a report this is unfair, since Constant offered the correlation of duty with right as just such an intermediate principle. As a verdict on the harm clause it comes close to Constant's own standard. Three of Kant's charges can be put in Constant's vocabulary.

The first is that truthfulness is the basis of all duties grounded in contract, a law that "is made wavering and useless if one grants it even the slightest exception" (8:427). Kant quotes nothing from the pages in which Constant defines a principle; his citations of Cramer begin with the passage on representation. "Schwankend" and "unnütz" are ordinary words, and I do not claim that Kant chose them as an echo. But they name Constant's two criteria. Fixity is where "all the utility" of a principle lies (68), and the arbitrary is where "everything is wavering" (78). Whatever Kant intended, Constant's theory obliges him to answer this charge, and he cannot answer it by saying that his clause is a modification rather than an exception, since a modification must be fixed too.

The second charge concerns imputation, but its premise serves Constant's standard. A truth harms others or not depending on what others then do. Kant's own variation makes the point: the friend may have slipped out, so that a lie sends the murderer to meet him, while the truth would have kept him searching the house until the neighbours came (8:427). Kant concludes that the liar answers for consequences he could not foresee. For Constant the lesson is different. A duty keyed to harm can be applied only by forecasting, so each speaker decides, case by case, whether the truth he is asked for will harm someone. That is the condition Constant called arbitrary: "only circumstances remain, and each person is judge of the circumstances" (78). Those who deal with someone bound only by Constant's clause cannot count on what he says, since he will lie whenever he judges the truth harmful, and the clause fails the test of chapter IX.

The third charge is that the clause releases too much. A witness whose truthful testimony will convict a guilty man tells a truth that harms another. By the clause, the court has no right to it and the witness no duty to give it. Constant could not accept this; he defended trial by jury and judicial forms throughout his career [@Constant1872, ch. XIX]. To exclude the witness he would need either an exception to his intermediate principle, which is the structure he denies, or a different key. Kant names the key. The "French philosopher" confused "the action by which someone harms (*nocet*) another by telling the truth, the admission of which he cannot avoid, with that by which he wrongs (*laedit*) him" (8:428). The witness harms the accused without wronging him. A clause keyed to wrong rather than harm would leave testimony untouched.

So the 1797 resolution fails, and it fails by Constant's standards: it is not fixed, and it does not exclude the arbitrary. Nothing in this shows that a duty indexed to persons must be an exception. Kant's further claims, that the duty "makes no distinction between persons" (8:429), that "a right to the truth" is "a word without sense" (8:426), and that the true principle must be "a priori recognized, hence apodictic" (8:429), a phrase he inserts into his quotation of Constant's maxim, state Kant's conception against Constant's. They do not follow from the internal critique. What the internal critique shows is that Constant needed a different key: wrong rather than harm.

# The principle the case needed {#sec-needed}

Constant's example is spare, but the pamphlet around it is not. Its first chapter describes leaders of the reaction who incited their followers "to the assassination of their accomplices" and made "national vengeance illegal and atrocious" (6). Chapter VII warns that if the royalists triumphed "proscription would be without end and without limits" (50), and calls on the friends of liberty to defend men "exalted in their opinions but not stained by crimes", whom some would make "a proscribed and terrible race, which would have no asylum on earth but beneath the ruins of the social order" (56–57). Chapter IX says of the Terror that its government "offered no protective form, no fixed law, nothing precise, determined, nothing therefore that could guarantee"; it was "founded on no law", and those who had massacred "without judgement or by arbitrary judgements" fell in turn: "they had put outside the law, and they were put outside the law" (90–91).

In this pamphlet a friend who has taken refuge in your house from those pursuing him is the *proscrit* seeking asylum, and his pursuers are the agents of proscription, whether they carry a decree of outlawry or belong to the bands of the reaction. The political setting has been noticed (above, @sec-intro; see also @Rousseliere2018). What the pamphlet adds is a vocabulary for it, and the vocabulary concerns law. The Terror was arbitrary because it rested on no law; its decrees had the form of law without the substance. Constant's 1797 clause does not use this vocabulary. Eighteen years later he did.

In the *Principes de politique* of 1815, chapter XVII discusses Rousseau's civil profession of faith, whose articles the sovereign may fix and whose unbelievers he may banish, not as impious but as unsociable. A footnote reports Rousseau's addition: whoever has publicly acknowledged the dogmas and behaves as if he did not believe them is to be punished with death, for "he has committed the greatest of crimes, he has lied before the laws".^[Rousseau, *Du contrat social*, IV.8, as paraphrased in Constant's note. I cite the 1815 text from Laboulaye's edition [@Constant1872], which reprints the *Principes* as the first part of the *Cours de politique constitutionnelle*.] Constant replies:

> But he who has the misfortune not to believe these dogmas cannot avow his doubts without exposing himself to banishment; and if his affections hold him back, if he has a family, a wife, children whom he hesitates to leave to rush into exile, is it not you, you alone, who force him to what you call the greatest of crimes, to lying before the laws? I will say, moreover, that in this circumstance this lie seems to me far from being a crime. *Quand de prétendues lois n'exigent de nous la vérité que pour nous proscrire, nous ne leur devons pas la vérité*: when pretended laws demand the truth of us only to proscribe us, we do not owe them the truth. [@Constant1872, 128–129 n. 1]

The text the note annotates goes on to ask what it matters that the sovereign does not strike me as impious if he strikes me as unsociable, or that authority abstains from theology "if it loses itself in a hypothetical morality, no less subtle, no less foreign to its natural jurisdiction" (129).

Two cautions. I know of no evidence that Constant read Kant's reply or had the 1797 exchange in mind, and the case is a demanded profession of belief, not a hunted friend. The claim is structural: here Constant states a principle about owed truth that has the key the 1797 clause lacked. Four features show it.

First, the lie in question is a declaration before the law. That is Kant's own hard case. His essay asks whether one is permitted to be untruthful in a statement "to which an unjust compulsion constrains him" (8:426), and Wood argues that its real subject is "the duty to speak truthfully in declarations in political contexts" [@Wood2011]. The note meets Kant where his position is strongest, in the legally demanded statement.

Second, the principle is keyed to wrong. The demand is made "only to proscribe us", and proscription is the paradigm wrong of Constant's politics. Nothing in the note turns on the truth's effects; a genuine law may demand truth that harms, as the court demands it of the witness.

Third, the principle is keyed to the title of the demand. The laws are *prétendues*, laws in name only, and "we do not owe them" the truth. The language of the 1797 definition survives, since a duty is owed to those with a right, but the right now belongs to authority acting within its jurisdiction, and a law that legislates belief is "foreign to its natural jurisdiction". Read this way, the right to the truth is not a property of propositions, which was Kant's complaint against the phrase: truth is not "a possession" granted to one and refused to another (8:428), and nothing about the questioner's will could make a proposition true or false (8:426). It is a title of the questioner, the standing to demand an answer. Constant's 1815 theory of sovereignty supplies the criterion for that standing: sovereignty "exists only in a limited and relative way", and "at the point where independence and individual existence begin, the jurisdiction of this sovereignty stops" [@Constant1872, 9].

Fourth, the principle covers the 1797 case. Assassins who want to know where your friend is so as to kill him demand the truth only in order to wrong him, and they lack even the pretence of law. The historical case behind the example, agents carrying a decree of outlawry, falls under the note's wording directly.

Does the 1815 principle pass Constant's test? Whether a demand comes from law within its jurisdiction, and whether its only purpose is proscription, are not forecasts of what others will do. They are features of the demand, settled by public rules about what authority may require, of the kind the whole of the 1815 *Principes* sets out to state. The court and its witness, and the declarations on which contracts rest, keep the reliance Kant cares about; the principle withholds truthfulness only from those who demand it in order to proscribe. It also passes Kant's distinction. The witness harms the accused but does not wrong him; the man who answers the proscriber's question lends himself to a wrong. And the note's rhetorical question, "is it not you, you alone, who force him", turns Kant's account of imputation around. For Kant the liar answers for whatever follows from his lie (8:427). For Constant, when the demand is a pretended law's, the author of the lie is the lawgiver who extorted it.

# What remains {#sec-remains}

Kant has a reply, and it is not about principles. In the *Doctrine of Right*, published earlier in 1797, the subject owes obedience to "the legislative power now existing, whatever its origin may be" (6:319). He may oppose its injustices with "complaints (*gravamina*), but no resistance" (6:319), and there can be no lawful resistance, because the question "who is to be judge in this dispute between people and sovereign" has no answer except one that makes the people judge in its own cause (6:320). On that view there is no category of pretended laws for a subject to identify; the judgement Constant's principle calls for is one the subject is not entitled to make. @Troitsky2016 links Kant's ban on lying to his ban on resistance. On the reading defended here the link runs through Constant's own principle, which turns on exactly the judgement of title that Kant's theory of right withholds from subjects.

The contrast is sharp at one point. Kant says the subject must obey the existing legislative power "whatever its origin may be" (6:319). Constant, in the chapter that states the limits of sovereignty, says that when any authority commits acts beyond its competence, "it matters little from what source it claims to derive" [@Constant1872, 9]. Both deny that origin settles the question, to opposite effect. For Kant origin cannot undo the duty to obey; for Constant origin cannot confer a title that the act's scope denies. Since a lie is not resistance by force, Kant's case against the lie must go through the essay's wrong to humanity in general, the corruption of declarations as the source of right (8:426). Constant's reply is available from the note: a pretended law is not part of that source, so truthfulness towards it does not sustain the institutions of declaration, any more than a decree of outlawry sustains the institutions of justice.

Constant's own view of who judges changed between 1797 and 1815, and the change concedes something to Kant. In 1797 definition was to yield a modification "which excludes all arbitrariness". In 1815, discussing the responsibility of subordinate agents who execute illegal orders, Constant argued that passive obedience cannot be maintained without restriction, but admitted: "Nor can you indicate with precision each circumstance in which obedience ceases to be a duty and becomes a crime." It is "impossible … to regulate everything, to write everything", and "whatever one does, there always remains in human affairs something discretionary" [@Constant1872, 94–95]. His answer was institutional: the residual judgement goes to juries, who exercise it once and have no permanent interest in power. That concedes Kant's point of 1793, that the application of rules needs a judgement that rules cannot exhaust (8:275), while locating the judgement where it is least arbitrary.

At the door there is no jury. But the judgement the 1815 principle needs differs from the one the 1797 clause needed. It is not a forecast of harm made by each speaker for each truth. It is a judgement about whether a demand has the title of law, of a kind Constant thought citizens must be able to make if limited sovereignty is to mean anything, and of a kind Kant thought they must not make if there is to be a civil condition at all.

That is where centring Constant leaves the murderer at the door. The case Kant made famous is a simplification of the one Constant described: a lone murderer in place of the agents of proscription, and a forced yes-or-no answer in place of a refuge. Constant's own 1797 answer to it fails his own standard, as Kant in effect showed. But the theory in which he set it was not expediency. It was a theory of principles as fixed rules against the arbitrary, and that theory, together with his politics of limited sovereignty, yields a principle that meets both his own standard and Kant's distinction between harming and wronging. Constant's question was never whether one may lie to save a friend. It was whether truth is owed to power that has exceeded its jurisdiction.
